grep "applicationName" | awk '{print $2}'

It's almost never necessary to pipe grep into awk. 

awk '/applicationName/ {print $2}'

Every AWK program is structured like this:

TEST 1 {ACTIONS}
TEST 2 {ACTIONS}
...

ACTIONS will be applied to every input record for which TEST succeeds. Omitting TEST means ACTIONS will be applied to every input record. Omitting ACTIONS means to print the successful input record.

testit() { ps -ef | awk '/$1/ {print $2}' | grep -v grep | xargs echo; }

You're trying to expand the $1 shell parameter inside single quotes. That's not going work. The single quotes are not part of the AWK program; they are there to protect the AWK program from shell expansions . In this case, you want the shell to expand $1. 

$ ( set -- poodle ; ps -ef | awk "/$1/ "'{print}' )
me 3111 3109 0 10:06 pts/0 00:00:00 awk /poodle/ {print}
$

The shell will expand any variable within double quotes; that's what we want for $1. The shell doesn't expand anything between single quotes; that's what we want for $2.

I have sent a number of people here, it's an interactive tutorial. Basically, with regex, at some point you just have to dive in. It's arcane, hard to learn, and unintuitive, but once you learn it, you can do some pretty amazing stuff. That being said, there is the old adage:

Some people, when confronted with a problem, think "I know, I'll use regular expressions." Now they have two problems.

Let's talk about some advanced usage of the shell itself (these examples I know work with Bash), which is well capable of doing a lot of stuff people abuse utilities like awk, grep, and cat for.

So say you want to list only particular files your current directory, like all of your jpegs. Most people seem to jump on the ls piped to grep. You probably don't need grep here though. Using a wildcard, the asterisk, the shell will expand everything ending with .jpg for you.

ls *.jpg

Ever needed to send a string to a program's standard input? If so, you might have echo'd it to a pipe to your program. No need for a pipe though.

someprogram <<< "This is going to someprogram's standard input"
someprogram < this_files_contents_going_to_stdin.txt

Ever wanted to silence or log all output? Redirect both standard output and standard error at the same time with the ampersand. Without that character, the shell willl redirect only standard output.

someprogram &>/dev/null
someprogram &>someprograms_log_file.txt

Another cool thing I pointed out to a voat user recently is the use of the shell to open and read a file for neat one-liners. You might have a list of file names in a file, and you want that list as arguments to some program. There are a few ways to go about this, including xargs abuse, but the last one is the most efficient:

cat file_list.txt | xargs someprogram
xargs someprogram < file_list.txt
someprogram $(< file_list.txt)

Or maybe you want the output of another program as some program's arguments. You can abuse xargs some more, or just use a subshell:

someotherprogram | xargs someprogram
someprogram $(someotherprogram)

I could probably list a few more neat things you can do with just the shell, but this is becoming a wall of text already. The tips I listed are just the ones I use regularly since learning them.
